issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette: James is a 77-year-old delivery driver who lives with his wife in a modest home on the edge of a quiet suburb. The night he was attacked, he was returning from a late-night run to deliver a batch of groceries to a downtown apartment complex. He had parked his truck on the curb, waited for the doorbell to ring, and when it did, a man in a dark hoodie lunged forward, striking James across the chest with a baseball bat. The blow sent him to the ground, his truck's engine sputtering in the background. In the instant after the attack, James could taste iron and hear the echo of the bat's impact. The shattering of his safety was so abrupt that he left the truck, ran home, and locked the doors to his house, his heart pounding against his ribs. From that night onward, James's thoughts became a battleground. He told himself that he could not trust the world; the street he had once felt safe in now felt like a minefield. He began to doubt his own judgment, questioning whether he could ever make the right decisions on the road or in his own home. "I can't even be sure that I'll be able to get there on time without being attacked again," he told his wife, who, though she loved him dearly, could see his eyes grow wary each time they crossed a dimly lit alley. The assault had shattered the beliefs that had guided him for decades: the idea that people were generally trustworthy, that the city's lights were safe, that his job was just a routine task. Those long-standing convictions had collapsed in the space of a single night, and he feared that if he let his mind wander back to the event, it would become too overwhelming to bear. In an effort to keep those memories at bay, James turned to a trio of coping tactics that have now defined his daily life. When a rumbling in his stomach threatened to grow into a rumbling roar, he would eat-an entire box of cereal, a few slices of pizza, sometimes even a whole bag of chips-just to fill the silence that the assault had carved out. "Food is a quiet," he would say, and his hands would clench around a bag of snack foods, as if that could swallow the terror. The act of eating also offered a distraction; the crunch of the bag was a small sound that pulled him away from the heavy, intrusive images that flickered in his mind. James also kept himself on the move, as though busyness could block out the assault. He would double-check routes, drive through back alleys he had never used before, and fill his time with extra deliveries, especially on nights when his truck's engine whined or his phone buzzed with messages. "If I'm busy, I won't have time to think," he told his wife, who watched him pace the living room as he planned his next route. And when a memory slipped into his thoughts-perhaps the taste of the bat or the scream of a neighbor-he would swallow it down with a gulp of water, forcing his attention back to the next step on his list. His mind became a shield of busyness and overeating, and he believed that this strategy would keep the assault from re-entering his consciousness. The consequences of these habits have piled up over the years. The extra weight he carried from overeating has led to frequent visits to the doctor, who warned him of high blood pressure and cholesterol. His wife has tried to talk to him about cutting back on the snacks, but he always deflects with a promise to "get it under control" after a long shift. James's relentless busyness at work has started to affect his safety on the road: in a rush to make a late delivery, he once nearly collided with a school bus on a slick night, only stopped at the last moment by the driver's quick reflexes. The incident left him feeling even more doubtful of his own capabilities, reinforcing the belief that he might not be able to drive safely without being caught in another attack. He reached out for therapy because he realized that his strategies, once simple shields, were now chains that held him back from living. He fears that his body may fail him if he keeps eating beyond his limits, and he worries that his marriage might dissolve if he can't find a way to be present with his wife instead of always being on the road or in the kitchen. Most of all, James is afraid that the assault will return, not only in memory but in a physical form that he cannot control. He hopes that a new way of looking at those fears will let him step off the road of busyness, let the food sit in a bowl rather than in his stomach, and finally confront the terror he has kept at bay for decades.
